title: Willowbrook Analytics — surge & hosting mode capacity evaluation
next_steps: Run 1-hour token/sec burst benchmark on Redwood hosted with their sample traces (Jonah to share test plan)
Share SOC 2 + ISO docs and KMS integration guide
Schedule technical deep dive (30–45m) for private deployment network topology — propose Wed next week
Provide preliminary pricing estimate for Dedicated capacity and surge buffer options
action_items: Jonah Park: share benchmark test plan & sample scripts by 2026-09-27
Ethan Cole: provide representative 1-week traffic trace and cost target by 2026-09-29
Ava Martinez: send SOC2 + compliance pack and draft quote by 2026-09-28
summary: Willowbrook runs an ingestion-heavy analytics assistant with intermittent high-throughput spikes. They need p95 < 300ms for 256-token streaming responses at 30 concurrent streams, and graceful degradation during token bursts. Primary constraint is cost per token and corporate data residency; they are evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Agreed next steps: share benchmark plan, collect traces, schedule private-deploy network deep dive.
transcript:
[00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone thanks for hopping on, we wanted to cover throughput and latency targets and figure the best hosting mode for Willowbrook.
[00:08] Priya Singh: Yeah thanks Ava, I know you got Jonah from infra — big topic for us is the p95 latency for streaming responses. We target sub-300ms for p95 on 256-token responses at roughly 30 concurrent user streams.
[00:20] Jonah Park: Right — just to clarify, is that 30 concurrent streams sustained, or bursty?
[00:24] Priya Singh: Mostly sustained during business hours but we see bursts up to 200 concurrent for short windows — like deploys or batch re-ingests.
[00:31] Luis Ortega: And to add, our cost target is tight. We're trying not to exceed current token cost by more than 35% while preserving latency SLOs.
[00:39] Jonah Park: Okay good, so two axes — steady-state concurrency (~30) and short token bursts (200). For streaming, p95 is often dominated by per-token latency and KV/cache hits. We usually look at prefix KV cache, batching, and continuous batching knobs.
[00:49] Hannah Kim: Quick question: does Redwood's hosted API support per-customer prefix caching or is that only on Dedicated/Private?
[00:55] Ava Martinez: Hosted supports multi-tenant prefix caching and tenant-aware KV cache on most model variants; Dedicated and Private give you isolation and more control over cache sizing and TTLs. There's also options for explicit warmup endpoints for predictable bursts.
[01:08] Ethan Cole: On the bursts — we can provide a traffic trace. We want you guys to run a tokens/sec benchmark using our trace if possible.
[01:15] Jonah Park: Absolutely. We'll run a 1-hour run with the trace, simulate the 30 sustained users and the burst windows. We'll measure p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and streaming latency per token. We'll also test with and without prefix KV caching enabled to show delta.
[01:26] Priya Singh: And quantization? We plan to use an LLM family that's quant-friendly but want to maintain quality. If quantized models drop latency but introduce hallucination risks, we need to see evals.
[01:36] Maya Ruiz: We can provide model recommendations and quantization profile suggestions tied to their eval sets — Redwood Optimize will run quality regressions on your prompt sets. For bursts we typically recommend int8 quantized variants for cost but keep an FP16 fallback for strict quality checks.
[01:47] Luis Ortega: For hosting decision — if Dedicated, what's the ramp for autoscaling during a burst? We need a fast scale or else fallback behavior must be graceful.
[01:55] Jonah Park: Dedicated supports reserved pools plus a burst buffer to Hosted for overflow. Autoscaling can be configured aggressively; you can set policy to scale by replica or by underlying GPU fractional capacity. Fallback options include routing to nearby regions, stepping down model size, or queueing with fast 429-based backpressure.
[02:08] Priya Singh: Data residency is another constraint. Some user logs must remain in our VPC.
[02:12] Ava Martinez: For Private deployments we run a customer-managed control plane; logs and KV cache can remain inside your VPC. Dedicated offers encryption-at-rest and customer-managed KMS integration. Hosted keeps metadata but we can offer contractual data residency terms for certain regions.
[02:25] Ethan Cole: What about audit logs and SSO? We require SAML SSO and audit trails for token usage per user.
[02:30] Maya Ruiz: SSO via SAML/SCIM is supported; audit logs are available in Redwood Console with token-level tags. For Private we can forward logs to your SIEM.
[02:40] Hannah Kim: For the benchmark, can you also measure cold KV misses vs warmed cache? Our prefix reuse rate is around 45% by our estimates.
[02:46] Jonah Park: Yes, we'll include cold/warm cache cases. We'll also run with different batch sizes; continuous batching typically improves throughput but slightly increases tail latency — we'll show that tradeoff.
[02:59] Priya Singh: How do you route requests across models if a variant is out of capacity? We don't want to degrade to a tiny model without notice.
[03:05] Jonah Park: Smart routing policies can do soft fallbacks: first try same model family in different capacity tier, then a bigger-sequence-optimized variant, then your chosen smaller fallback with response annotated. We also have canaries and rollout policies to avoid surprise downgrades.
[03:19] Luis Ortega: Are those fallback annotations accessible via API so we can log them?
[03:22] Ava Martinez: Yes, the response metadata includes model_id and fallback_reason. That can be instrumented into your telemetry.
[03:29] Priya Singh: From a procurement perspective we'd need pricing for Dedicated with a 20% burst buffer reserved and a Hosted overflow cap.
[03:36] Ava Martinez: We'll include a dedicated quote with reserved capacity, and modeled cost scenarios for burst buffer sizes. We'll also show per-token cost delta between quantized and FP16 variants.
[03:45] Ethan Cole: One more technical piece: with streaming we care about token/sec and p95 of inter-token latency. Does Redwood expose per-token timing in traces?
[03:52] Jonah Park: Yes, our tracing captures token emit timestamps; we'll give you sample traces and a CSV with inter-token latencies. That helps diagnose server-side scheduling vs network jitter.
[04:03] Hannah Kim: And network topology for Private — we need to know egress patterns and port requirements for on-prem control plane.
[04:09] Maya Ruiz: We'll bring that to the deep dive. Typically the control plane needs outbound HTTPS to Redwood endpoints and gRPC ports for model traffic; we'll provide a one-page network checklist.
[04:18] Priya Singh: Any known gotchas for 200-concurrent short bursts?
[04:22] Jonah Park: For that profile, warm KV cache and pre-warmed model slots help a lot. If you rely on very long sequences, memory pressure can increase latency. Also beware small-batch quantized kernels that sometimes regress on hallucination — we'll test quality.
[04:34] Luis Ortega: Ok. What's the timeline?
[04:36] Ava Martinez: Jonah will run the benchmark as soon as you share the trace and we'll aim to have results in 3–4 business days. Then we propose a 45-minute private-deploy topology call the following week.
[04:46] Priya Singh: Sounds good. Please include a notes section in the benchmark with config: model name, batch size, quantization flag, cache TTL, and concurrency profile.
[04:55] Jonah Park: Will do. We'll also include the raw logs so you can inspect token-level metrics.
[05:01] Ava Martinez: Great, recap — action items: Jonah share test plan; Ethan send traces and SLO target doc; Ava send SOC2/compliance pack and draft quote. We'll follow up with calendar invites. Thanks everyone.
[05:14] Priya Singh: Thanks all, appreciate it.
[05:16] [call ends]
